m0.title: Hello, Python
m0.anchor: Install Python + run your first .py file

m1.title: Variables + print
m1.anchor: Store member names; f-strings for "My bias is…"

concept.intro: A variable is a named box for a value; print() is how your program talks back. An f-string — f"My bias is {name}" — drops variables straight into text. Everything runs on YOUR machine: write the file, run it in the terminal, compare outputs here.

examples.why: A variable stores a value; print() writes it to the terminal.
Python does the math right inside print().
An f-string drops a variable into the middle of text. Note the f before the quote.

exercises.title: Print your bias
exercises.prompt: Store the name Jungkook in a variable, then print it. Run the file in your terminal and compare.
hints: Which tool stores a value so you can reuse it later? A variable.
Shape:  name = "..."  on one line, then  print(name)  on the next.
approachChecklist: Did you print the variable, or retype the string inside print()?
Would your code still work if the name changed?

exercises.prompt: BTS debuted in 2013. Print the sentence below — the 13 must be computed by Python, not typed by you.
exercises.expectedOutput: BTS have been active for 13 years
hints: Math works inside an f-string: {2026 - debut}.
Shape:  debut = 2013  then  print(f"... {2026 - debut} ...")
exercises.solution:
debut = 2013
print(f"BTS have been active for {2026 - debut} years")
approachChecklist: Is 13 computed, or hard-coded?
Does your spacing match the expected output exactly?

exercises.title: Bias and wrecker
exercises.prompt: Two variables, exactly one line of output.
hints: Two variables can live in one f-string.
Shape:  print(f"Bias: {a} / Wrecker: {b}")
approachChecklist: One print or two? One output line means one print.
Exact spaces around the slash?

concept.intro: Numbers need no quotes. Python adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides with + - * and /, and // keeps only the whole part. Anything a calculator can do, print() can show — and f-strings can do the math mid-sentence.

examples.why: No quotes means numbers — and minus works on them.
* multiplies. Variables holding numbers behave like numbers.
/ always gives a decimal answer (a float), even for 10 / 5.
// is whole-number division: it chops the decimal off.

concept.intro: A string is text in quotes, and it carries tools called methods: chant.upper() returns a shouting copy of chant. Two built-ins matter now too — len() counts characters, and [start:stop] slices out a piece (the stop position is not included).

examples.why: .upper() returns a capitals copy; the original stays lowercase.
len() counts characters, spaces included.
in asks "is this inside that?" — the answer is True or False.
A slice [0:4] takes positions 0, 1, 2, 3 — the stop is not included.

m4.title: Errors 101
m4.anchor: Read tracebacks; fix deliberately broken snippets

concept.intro: Errors are not punishment — they are Python telling you exactly where it gave up. Read the LAST line first: the error type and its message. The lines above name the file and line; a ^ arrow points near the problem. Every exercise below hands you broken code to fix.

examples.output:
File "hello.py", line 1
    print("Dynamite)
          ^
SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 1)
examples.why: A SyntaxError happens before the program even runs. The arrow points at the unfinished string — a quote is missing.

examples.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "hello.py", line 1, in <module>
    print(bias)
NameError: name 'bias' is not defined
examples.why: NameError means a name was used before it got a value. Last line first, always.

examples.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "hello.py", line 1, in <module>
    print("7" + 7)
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
examples.why: TypeError: text and numbers refuse to glue with +. Quotes made the first 7 text.

exercises.title: Fix the quote
exercises.prompt: This crashes:  print("Butter)  — run it, read the traceback, fix it so it prints the song title.
hints: Read the last traceback line: unterminated string literal.
Every opening quote needs a closing quote before the ).
approachChecklist: Could you have found it from the ^ arrow alone?
Read the last traceback line out loud — does it describe the fix?

exercises.title: Fix the name
exercises.prompt: This crashes:  member = "Jin"  then  print(Member)  — fix it so it prints the name.
hints: NameError: name Member is not defined. Capital letters matter.
The variable you made is member, all lowercase.
approachChecklist: Are member and Member the same name to Python?
Which traceback line told you the answer?

exercises.title: Fix the type
exercises.prompt: This crashes:  print("Debut: " + 2013)  — fix it so it prints the line below.
hints: TypeError: text will not + with a number.
An f-string prints numbers inside text with no glue needed.
approachChecklist: f-string, or quotes around 2013 — both work. Which did you pick?
Why exactly did + fail here?

exitExercise.title: Exit — two bugs, one line
exitExercise.prompt: This snippet hides two bugs:  chant = "borahae  (missing quote)  then  print(chant.uper())  (misspelled method). Fix both.
approachChecklist: Which bug did Python report first — and why only that one?

m5.title: Lists
m5.anchor: The members list — indexing, append, slicing the rap line

concept.intro: A list keeps things in order inside one variable. Positions start at 0, len() counts items, .append() adds to the end, and [start:stop] slices a run of neighbours. Meet the members list — you will use it for the rest of the course.

examples.why: Positions start at 0 — members[0] is the first item.
len() works on lists too: it counts items, not letters.
The slice takes positions 4, 5, 6 — stop 7 is not included. Printing a list shows brackets and quotes.
.append() adds one item to the end, in place.

exercises.title: Who is members[3]?
exercises.prompt: Using the full members list from the examples, print the member at position 3. Predict first, then check.
hints: Count from 0: RM is 0, Jin is 1…
Shape:  print(members[3])
approachChecklist: Did your prediction match?
Which position is Jungkook at?

exercises.title: Build a setlist
exercises.prompt: Start a list with only Mic Drop, append Fire, then print the whole list. Brackets and quotes count — match exactly.
hints: .append() adds one item to the end.
Print the LIST itself, not each song.
approachChecklist: Did you print the list once, or song by song?
Python prints single quotes — did that trip your match?

exercises.title: Slice the maknae line
exercises.prompt: Slice Jimin, V and Jungkook out of the members list and print the slice.
hints: They sit at positions 4, 5 and 6.

exitExercise.title: Exit — the maknae
exitExercise.prompt: Using the members list and an f-string, print the line below by looking the name up by its position.
approachChecklist: Position 6, or len(members) - 1 — both reach the end. Which did you use?

concept.intro: if runs a block only when a test is True. The indented lines under the colon are the block. == asks "are these equal?" (one = stores, two == compare), elif tries the next test, else catches everything left. Python takes the FIRST true branch and skips the rest.

examples.why: The indented line runs only because the test is True.
== compares. One = stores a value; two == ask a question.
else runs when the test fails — exactly one branch ever runs.
2018 fails the first test, passes the second — and the rest is skipped.

exercises.title: Take my money
exercises.prompt: price = 4500. If it is more than 4000, print Too pricey — otherwise print Take my money.
hints: > compares numbers; the test goes right after if.
Shape:  if price > 4000:  indented print, then  else:  and another.
approachChecklist: What prints if you change price to 3000?
Is each print indented under its branch?

exercises.title: Which era?
exercises.prompt: year = 2013. Build the ladder: before 2016 print School trilogy, before 2020 print Love Yourself era, otherwise print A recent era.
hints: if, then elif, then else — three branches, one colon each.
Shape:  if year < 2016: … elif year < 2020: … else: …
approachChecklist: Why does 2013 NOT also print the elif branch?
Trace year = 2019 by hand before running it.

exercises.title: Bias check
exercises.prompt: name = "Jimin". If name equals Jimin print Same bias! — otherwise print Respect.
hints: Two equals signs compare; one stores.
Shape:  if name == "Jimin":
approachChecklist: What happens with name = "V"?
What does a single = inside the if do? Try it — read the error.

exitExercise.title: Exit — era ladder, new year
exitExercise.prompt: year = 2022. Same ladder shape as practice: before 2016 → Early era, before 2020 → Middle era, otherwise → Recent era.
approachChecklist: Which two tests did 2022 fail before landing in else?

m7.title: for loops
m7.anchor: Fan chant one name per line; counting songs

concept.intro: for repeats a block once per item in a list. The loop variable — for name in members — holds the current item and changes every pass. range(3) makes the numbers 0, 1, 2, handy for "do this N times". Indented lines run every pass; unindented lines run once, after.

examples.output:
RM
Jin
Suga
J-Hope
Jimin
V
Jungkook
examples.why: One print, seven lines — the block runs once per member.
Any list works, and f-strings work inside the loop.
range(3) counts 0, 1, 2 — three numbers, starting at 0.

examples.code:
members = ["RM", "Jin", "Suga", "J-Hope", "Jimin", "V", "Jungkook"]
count = 0
for name in members:
    count = count + 1
print(count)
examples.why: The counter grows once per pass. The final print is unindented — outside the loop — so it runs once.

exercises.title: The full fan chant
exercises.prompt: Loop over the members list and print each name with an ! on its own line.
exercises.expectedOutput:
RM!
Jin!
Suga!
J-Hope!
Jimin!
V!
Jungkook!
hints: One print inside the loop handles all seven.
Shape:  for name in members:  then  print(f"{name}!")
approachChecklist: A loop, or seven copied prints? Be honest.
What changes if you unindent the print?

exercises.title: Encore ×3
exercises.prompt: Print Encore! exactly three times using range — not three print lines.
hints: range(3) runs a block three times.
Shape:  for i in range(3):
approachChecklist: range, or copy-paste?
What does i hold each pass, even though you never printed it?

exercises.prompt: Loop over ["Jimin", "V", "Jungkook"] with a counter, then print the count after the loop.
hints: Start count = 0 BEFORE the loop; add 1 inside it.

What would it print indented inside?

exitExercise.title: Exit — now playing
exitExercise.prompt: Loop over ["Dynamite", "Butter", "Fire"] and print each one as  Now playing: title.

concept.intro: while repeats as long as its test stays True — so something inside must change, or it never ends (Ctrl+C stops a runaway loop). input("…") shows a prompt, waits for typing, and hands back what was typed — always as text. Exercises tell you EXACTLY what to type so outputs match.

examples.code:
n = 1
while n <= 3:
    print(n)
    n = n + 1
examples.why: n grows each pass; at 4 the test fails and the loop ends.

examples.code:
answer = input("Bias? ")
print(f"{answer} is a great pick")
examples.output:
Bias? Jimin
Jimin is a great pick
examples.why: You typed Jimin. input() shows the prompt, waits, and returns the typed text — which also appears on the prompt line.

examples.code:
guess = ""
while guess != "V":
    guess = input("King of duality? ")
print("Correct!")
examples.output:
King of duality? Jin
King of duality? V
Correct!
examples.why: You typed Jin, then V. The loop keeps asking until the test fails.

exercises.title: Countdown
exercises.prompt: Count 3, 2, 1 with a while loop, then print Comeback! after it ends.
hints: Start n = 3; loop while n >= 1; shrink n inside.
The Comeback! print is unindented — after the loop.
exercises.solution:
n = 3
while n >= 1:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
print("Comeback!")
approachChecklist: What exactly stops the loop?
Move the last print inside — what changes?

exercises.title: Ask the bias
exercises.prompt: Ask with input("Bias? ") and echo the answer back. When it asks, type exactly: Jungkook
exercises.expectedOutput:

approachChecklist: Why does Jungkook appear on the first line too? Your typing is part of the terminal.
The space after ?  is part of the prompt — did it match?

exercises.title: The magic word
exercises.prompt: Keep asking  Say the magic word:  until the answer is borahae, then print Doors open! When it asks, type exactly: army — then: borahae
exercises.expectedOutput:

Say the magic word: borahae
Doors open!
hints: The test compares the LAST answer:  while word != "borahae":
Start word = "" so the loop has something to test the first time.
exercises.solution:
word = ""
while word != "borahae":
    word = input("Say the magic word: ")
print("Doors open!")
approachChecklist: Why does word = "" make the loop start?
What happens if you type borahae first? Trace it.

exitExercise.title: Exit — find the maknae
exitExercise.prompt: Keep asking  Maknae?  until the answer is Jungkook, then print Correct! When it asks, type exactly: Jimin — then: Jungkook

m9.title: Dicts
m9.anchor: One song as a dict; look up album by title

concept.intro: A dict stores labelled values: key on the left, value on the right. Look a value up with square brackets and the KEY — song["title"] — not a position. Assigning to a new key adds it, and  "album" in song  asks whether a key exists.

examples.code:
song = {"title": "Spring Day", "album": "You Never Walk Alone", "year": 2017}
print(song["title"])
examples.why: Square brackets with the KEY, not a position number.
Values can be any type — this one is a number.
Assigning to a key that does not exist yet adds it.
in checks the KEYS — this dict has no album key.

exercises.title: Look up the album
exercises.prompt: song = {"title": "Spring Day", "album": "You Never Walk Alone", "year": 2017}. Print the line below using two lookups.
exercises.expectedOutput: Spring Day is on You Never Walk Alone
hints: Both values come out with ["…"] lookups.
Store each lookup in a variable first, then one f-string.
exercises.solution:
song = {"title": "Spring Day", "album": "You Never Walk Alone", "year": 2017}
title = song["title"]
album = song["album"]
print(f"{title} is on {album}")
approachChecklist: Lookups by key, not retyped values?
Could you do it without the helper variables?

exercises.title: Add the mood
exercises.prompt: Same song dict. Add a mood key with the value hopeful, then print it back out.
hints: Assign to a key that does not exist yet:  song["mood"] = …
Then print song["mood"].
approachChecklist: Adding and updating a key look identical — why is that fine?
What happens when you print a key that does not exist? Try it: KeyError.

exercises.title: Song card

hints: Two prints, one lookup each.
Inside an f-string, quote keys with SINGLE quotes: {song['title']}
approachChecklist: Why single quotes for the key inside the f-string?
Helper variables would also work — which reads better to you?

exitExercise.prompt: Make a dict for the song Butter, released 2021, and print the line below from lookups.
approachChecklist: Both values from the dict, not retyped?

concept.intro: def gives a block a name so you can run it whenever you like. Parameters are its inputs; return hands a value back to the caller. Defining does nothing by itself — the CALL is what runs it. This is where your code stops being a script and starts being tools.

examples.why: def defines the tool; the last line actually uses it.
return sends the True/False back to whoever asked.
A return ends the function immediately — the second return is the fallback.

exercises.title: Greeting function
exercises.prompt: Write greet(name) that prints  Annyeong, name!  — then call it with RM.
hints: def greet(name):  then an indented print.
Nothing prints until you CALL greet("RM") at the bottom.
approachChecklist: Did you remember the call at the bottom?
Call it twice with different names — zero extra work.

exercises.title: Double chant
exercises.prompt: Write chant(name) that prints the name on two lines, then call it with V.
hints: Two prints inside the function — or one small loop.
The body is everything indented under def.
approachChecklist: Loop or two prints — which did you pick, and why?
What does chant("Jin") print now?

exercises.title: Era function
exercises.prompt: Write era(year) that RETURNS Early for years before 2016 and Later otherwise. Print era(2014).
hints: return sends the word back; the print happens at the call.

Returning vs printing inside — what is the difference?

exitExercise.title: Exit — rap line check
exitExercise.prompt: Write is_rap_line(name) that returns True when the name is in ["RM", "Suga", "J-Hope"]. Print is_rap_line("Suga").

m11.title: Combining it all
m11.anchor: Lists of dicts + loops + functions together

concept.intro: The final shape: a list of dicts — every song is a dict, the catalogue is a list of them. Loop over the list and each pass hands you one dict; add if to filter, a counter to count, and a function to wrap it up. This is what real data looks like.

examples.code:
songs = [
    {"title": "Fire", "year": 2016, "mood": "hype"},
    {"title": "Spring Day", "year": 2017, "mood": "nostalgic"},
    {"title": "Dynamite", "year": 2020, "mood": "hype"},
    {"title": "Life Goes On", "year": 2020, "mood": "calm"},
]
for song in songs:
    print(song["title"])
examples.output:
Fire
Spring Day
Dynamite
Life Goes On
examples.why: Each pass, song is one whole dict — so key lookups work inside the loop.
Loop + if = a filter. Only matching passes reach the print.

examples.code:
songs = [
    {"title": "Fire", "year": 2016, "mood": "hype"},
    {"title": "Spring Day", "year": 2017, "mood": "nostalgic"},
    {"title": "Dynamite", "year": 2020, "mood": "hype"},
    {"title": "Life Goes On", "year": 2020, "mood": "calm"},
]
count = 0
for song in songs:
    if song["mood"] == "hype":
        count = count + 1
print(count)
examples.why: Loop + if + counter = counting by rule. Print sits outside the loop.
return ends the search on the first hit — a find-first tool.

m12.title: Capstone — the quiz app
m12.anchor: Terminal BTS quiz or setlist builder, demo-ready

concept.intro: The dream project: a terminal BTS quiz you can demo to friends. Nothing new to learn — variables, input(), if, loops and functions are the whole toolkit. Build it in three milestones; the exit is one full session that matches the transcript, typed inputs and all.

examples.code:
def ask(question, answer):
    guess = input(question)
    return guess == answer

print(ask("Maknae? ", "Jungkook"))
examples.why: You typed Jungkook. One function can run ANY question — prompt and answer are parameters.
A counter plus an f-string is your whole scoreboard.

exercises.prompt: Print the title, ask for a name, greet. When it asks, type exactly: Riya
exercises.expectedOutput:

hints: Three lines: a print, an input, an f-string print.
The typed Riya appears on the prompt line — that is normal.
exercises.solution:
print("BTS QUIZ")
name = input("Your name? ")
print(f"Welcome, {name}!")
approachChecklist: Prompt spacing exact?
Module 01 skills, nothing more — feel that?

hints: if guess == "Jungkook":  score = score + 1
score starts at 0 BEFORE the question.

guess = input("Maknae? ")
if guess == "Jungkook":
    score = score + 1
print(f"Score: {score}/1")
approachChecklist: What prints if you answer wrong?
Where must score = 0 sit, and why?

exercises.prompt: Three questions, one score, one final line. When it asks, type exactly: Jungkook — then: 2013 — then: RM
exercises.expectedOutput:

hints: Repeating the if block three times is fine — or reuse the ask() function from the examples.
input() returns TEXT: compare the year to "2013" in quotes.
approachChecklist: Why "2013" in quotes?

exitExercise.title: Exit — the demo session
exitExercise.prompt: The full app: title, name, three questions, score line, sign-off. One answer below is wrong on purpose — scoring must survive it. When it asks, type exactly: Riya — then: Jungkook — then: 2014 — then: RM
exitExercise.expectedOutput:
BTS QUIZ
Your name? Riya
Maknae? Jungkook
Debut year? 2014
Leader? RM
Riya, you scored 2/3
Borahae!
exitExercise.solution:
def ask(question, answer):
    guess = input(question)
